notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • A scientific law describes a consistent relationship or pattern observed in nature.
  • Scientific laws are based on repeated observations and experiments.
  • Many scientific laws are expressed mathematically.
  • A scientific law describes what happens under specified conditions.
  • A scientific theory mainly explains how or why a phenomenon occurs.
  • A theory does not automatically become a law after accumulating more evidence.
  • Scientific laws may have specified conditions or limits of applicability.
  • Laws of physics, chemistry and biology form the basis of many technologies.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Scientific Law → Describes a consistent relationship.

Scientific Theory → Explains phenomena.

2. Newton's First Law of Motion
  • Newton's First Law is also called the Law of Inertia.
  • A body remains at rest or continues in uniform straight-line motion unless acted upon by a net external force.
  • Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist change in its state of motion.
  • Greater mass generally means greater inertia.
  • The first law establishes the concept of force as something that changes motion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton I → Law of Inertia

3. Types of Inertia
  • Inertia of rest is the tendency of a body at rest to remain at rest.
  • Inertia of motion is the tendency of a moving body to continue moving with the same velocity.
  • Inertia of direction is the tendency of a body to resist change in its direction of motion.
  • Passengers falling backward when a bus suddenly starts illustrates inertia of rest.
  • Passengers falling forward when a moving bus suddenly stops illustrates inertia of motion.
  • Mud flying tangentially from a rotating tyre illustrates inertia of direction.
4. Newton's Second Law
  • Newton's Second Law relates force to the rate of change of momentum.
  • Force is proportional to the rate of change of momentum.
  • For constant mass, Newton's Second Law becomes F = ma.
  • F represents force.
  • m represents mass.
  • a represents acceleration.
  • The SI unit of force is newton.
  • One newton is the force required to accelerate a mass of 1 kg at 1 m/s².
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton II → F = ma

5. Newton's Third Law
  • Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
  • Action and reaction forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction.
  • Action and reaction act on different bodies.
  • Rocket propulsion is based on Newton's Third Law.
  • Recoil of a gun illustrates Newton's Third Law.
  • Walking is possible because the foot pushes the ground backward and the ground pushes the body forward.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Action and reaction do not cancel each other because they act on different bodies.

6. Law of Conservation of Momentum
  • Total momentum of an isolated system remains constant.
  • Momentum is the product of mass and velocity.
  • Momentum is represented by p.
  • p = mv.
  • The SI unit of momentum is kg m/s.
  • Conservation of momentum follows from Newton's laws.
  • Recoil of a gun demonstrates conservation of momentum.
  • Rocket motion also involves conservation of momentum.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Momentum → p = mv → Conserved in isolated system

7. Law of Conservation of Energy
  • Energy can neither be created nor destroyed in an isolated system.
  • Energy can be transformed from one form to another.
  • Total energy remains constant.
  • Potential energy can convert into kinetic energy.
  • Electrical energy can convert into heat, light or mechanical energy.
  • Chemical energy in food is converted into useful biological energy and heat.
  • Conservation of energy is one of the fundamental principles of physics.
📌 Remember

Energy → Not created or destroyed → Only transformed

8. Law of Conservation of Mass
  • The Law of Conservation of Mass is associated with Antoine Lavoisier.
  • In a chemical reaction, mass is neither created nor destroyed in a closed system.
  • The total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products.
  • The law forms an important basis of chemical equations.
  • Chemical equations are balanced to obey conservation of mass.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lavoisier → Conservation of Mass

9. Einstein's Mass-Energy Relation
  • Albert Einstein established the equivalence of mass and energy.
  • The relation is E = mc².
  • E represents energy.
  • m represents mass.
  • c represents the speed of light.
  • A small amount of mass can correspond to a very large amount of energy.
  • Nuclear fission and fusion involve measurable mass-energy conversion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Einstein → E = mc²

10. Universal Law of Gravitation
  • Newton formulated the universal law of gravitation.
  • Every mass attracts every other mass.
  • Gravitational force is directly proportional to the product of the masses.
  • Gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
  • The relation is F = Gm₁m₂/r².
  • G is the universal gravitational constant.
  • Gravity keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
  • Gravity keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton → Gravitation → F = Gm₁m₂/r²

11. Inverse Square Law
  • An inverse square relationship varies inversely with the square of distance.
  • Gravitational force follows an inverse square law.
  • Electrostatic force also follows an inverse square law.
  • Light intensity from an ideal point source decreases approximately according to an inverse square relationship.
  • Doubling distance reduces an inverse-square quantity to one-fourth.
📌 Remember

Distance × 2 → Effect becomes 1/4

Distance × 3 → Effect becomes 1/9

12. Kepler's First Law
  • Johannes Kepler formulated the laws of planetary motion.
  • Kepler's First Law states that planets move in elliptical orbits.
  • The Sun lies at one focus of each planetary ellipse.
📌 Remember

Kepler I → Ellipse

13. Kepler's Second Law
  • A line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal intervals of time.
  • A planet moves faster when closer to the Sun.
  • A planet moves slower when farther from the Sun.
📌 Remember

Kepler II → Equal Areas in Equal Times

14. Kepler's Third Law
  • The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.
  • T² ∝ a³.
  • Planets farther from the Sun generally take longer to complete an orbit.
📌 Remember

Kepler III → T² ∝ a³

15. Hooke's Law
  • Hooke's Law describes elastic deformation within the elastic limit.
  • Extension is directly proportional to the applied force within the elastic limit.
  • It is commonly written as F = kx.
  • k is the spring constant.
  • x is the extension or compression.
  • Robert Hooke formulated Hooke's Law.
  • The law ceases to apply after the elastic limit is exceeded.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hooke → F = kx → Elastic Limit

16. Pascal's Law
  • Pascal's Law deals with pressure in enclosed fluids.
  • Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.
  • Blaise Pascal is associated with Pascal's Law.
  • Hydraulic presses work on Pascal's Law.
  • Hydraulic brakes work on Pascal's Law.
  • Hydraulic lifts work on Pascal's Law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pascal → Confined Fluid → Hydraulic Machines

17. Archimedes' Principle
  • Archimedes' Principle deals with buoyancy.
  • A body immersed wholly or partially in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force.
  • The buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced.
  • Archimedes of Syracuse is associated with this principle.
  • Ships float because of buoyant force.
  • Hydrometers operate using principles of buoyancy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Archimedes → Buoyancy → Weight of displaced fluid

18. Law of Floatation
  • A floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight.
  • A body floats when the buoyant force balances its weight.
  • Ships made of dense materials can float because their overall average density can be lower than that of water.
  • Submarines control buoyancy using ballast tanks.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Archimedes' Principle → Buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid.

Law of Floatation → Floating body displaces its own weight of fluid.

19. Bernoulli's Principle
  • Bernoulli's principle relates fluid speed and pressure.
  • In a steady-flowing fluid, an increase in speed is associated with a decrease in static pressure under appropriate conditions.
  • Daniel Bernoulli is associated with this principle.
  • Atomisers use Bernoulli-related pressure effects.
  • Venturimeters operate using Bernoulli's principle.
  • Aerodynamic lift involves pressure, momentum change and airflow effects; Bernoulli's principle is one useful part of its explanation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Bernoulli → Faster Fluid → Lower Static Pressure

20. Continuity Equation
  • The continuity equation expresses conservation of mass in fluid flow.
  • For an incompressible fluid, A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
  • A represents cross-sectional area.
  • v represents flow speed.
  • Fluid speed increases when an incompressible fluid passes through a narrower section.
📌 Remember

Smaller area → Greater fluid speed

21. Torricelli's Law
  • Torricelli's law describes the speed of efflux of a liquid from an opening.
  • Efflux speed is given approximately by v = √(2gh).
  • h is the height of liquid above the opening.
  • Evangelista Torricelli is associated with this law.
  • The relation resembles the speed acquired by a body falling through height h.
22. Boyle's Law
  • Boyle's Law applies to a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature.
  • Pressure is inversely proportional to volume.
  • P ∝ 1/V.
  • Therefore, PV = constant.
  • Robert Boyle is associated with Boyle's Law.
  • Decreasing volume increases pressure when temperature is constant.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Boyle → Constant Temperature → PV = Constant

23. Charles's Law
  • Charles's Law applies to a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure.
  • Volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
  • V ∝ T.
  • Therefore, V/T = constant.
  • Temperature must be expressed in kelvin.
  • Jacques Charles is associated with Charles's Law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Charles → Constant Pressure → V/T = Constant

24. Gay-Lussac's Pressure Law
  • At constant volume, pressure of a fixed mass of gas is directly proportional to absolute temperature.
  • P ∝ T.
  • Therefore, P/T = constant.
  • Temperature must be expressed in kelvin.
  • Heating a gas in a rigid sealed container increases its pressure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Constant Volume → P/T = Constant

25. Avogadro's Law
  • At constant temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of molecules.
  • Volume is directly proportional to the amount of gas in moles.
  • V ∝ n.
  • Amedeo Avogadro proposed this relationship.
  • Avogadro's constant is approximately 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Avogadro → Equal gas volumes → Equal number of molecules

26. Combined Gas Law
  • Boyle's, Charles's and pressure laws can be combined.
  • For a fixed amount of gas, PV/T = constant.
  • Therefore, P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.
  • Temperature must be expressed on an absolute scale.
27. Ideal Gas Equation
  • The ideal gas equation is PV = nRT.
  • P represents pressure.
  • V represents volume.
  • n represents number of moles.
  • R is the universal gas constant.
  • T is absolute temperature.
  • Real gases approximate ideal behaviour best at relatively low pressure and high temperature.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ideal Gas → PV = nRT

28. Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
  • In a mixture of non-reacting gases, total pressure equals the sum of the partial pressures.
  • Ptotal = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ + ...
  • John Dalton formulated the law of partial pressures.
  • Partial pressure is the pressure a gas would exert if it alone occupied the container under the same conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dalton → Total Pressure = Sum of Partial Pressures

29. Graham's Law of Diffusion
  • Graham's Law relates the rate of diffusion or effusion of gases to molar mass.
  • The rate is inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass.
  • Lighter gases diffuse or effuse faster than heavier gases.
  • Thomas Graham formulated the law.
📌 Remember

Lower molar mass → Faster diffusion

30. Law of Definite Proportions
  • The Law of Definite Proportions is associated with Joseph Proust.
  • A pure chemical compound always contains the same elements in the same fixed proportion by mass.
  • Water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed mass ratio.
  • The law is also called the Law of Constant Composition.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Proust → Definite Proportions → Fixed Composition

31. Law of Multiple Proportions
  • The Law of Multiple Proportions is associated with John Dalton.
  • When two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of the other are in simple whole-number ratios.
  • The law supported Dalton's atomic theory.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Dalton → Multiple Proportions

32. Law of Reciprocal Proportions
  • The Law of Reciprocal Proportions is associated with Jeremias Benjamin Richter.
  • It describes relationships between masses of elements that separately combine with a fixed mass of another element.
  • The combining masses are related in the same or simple multiples of the ratio in which those elements combine with each other.
  • The law contributed to early quantitative chemistry.
33. Gay-Lussac's Law of Combining Volumes
  • Gases react in simple whole-number ratios by volume when measured at the same temperature and pressure.
  • Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac formulated the law.
  • The law helped develop molecular ideas in chemistry.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Gay-Lussac Pressure Law → P ∝ T at constant volume.

Gay-Lussac Combining Volumes Law → Simple whole-number gas volume ratios.

34. First Law of Thermodynamics
  • The First Law of Thermodynamics is based on conservation of energy.
  • Heat supplied to a system can change its internal energy and/or do work.
  • A common form is ΔU = Q − W when W is work done by the system.
  • Energy is conserved in thermodynamic processes.
  • A perpetual-motion machine of the first kind would violate the First Law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

First Law → Conservation of Energy

35. Zeroth Law of Thermodynamics
  • The Zeroth Law establishes the concept of thermal equilibrium.
  • If body A is in thermal equilibrium with body B, and B with C, then A is in thermal equilibrium with C.
  • The Zeroth Law provides the logical basis for temperature measurement.
  • Thermometers operate using the concept of thermal equilibrium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Zeroth Law → Thermal Equilibrium → Temperature

36. Second Law of Thermodynamics
  • The Second Law describes the natural direction of thermodynamic processes.
  • Heat does not spontaneously flow from a colder body to a hotter body.
  • No heat engine can convert all absorbed heat completely into work in a cyclic process.
  • Entropy of an isolated system tends not to decrease.
  • A perpetual-motion machine of the second kind would violate the Second Law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Second Law → Direction of Heat Flow + Entropy

37. Third Law of Thermodynamics
  • The Third Law concerns entropy near absolute zero.
  • The entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero.
  • Absolute zero is 0 K.
  • Absolute zero corresponds to approximately −273.15°C.
  • Absolute zero cannot be reached by a finite sequence of ordinary thermodynamic processes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Third Law → Absolute Zero

38. Newton's Law of Cooling
  • The rate of cooling of a body is approximately proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings under suitable conditions.
  • Larger temperature difference generally produces faster cooling.
  • The law works best for relatively small temperature differences under controlled conditions.
39. Stefan-Boltzmann Law
  • The total radiant energy emitted per unit area by an ideal black body is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature.
  • E ∝ T⁴.
  • The constant of proportionality is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant.
  • Hotter bodies radiate much more energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stefan-Boltzmann → Radiation → T⁴

40. Wien's Displacement Law
  • Wien's displacement law relates black-body temperature to the wavelength of maximum emission.
  • λmax T = constant.
  • As temperature increases, the peak wavelength becomes shorter.
  • Hotter stars tend to emit more strongly at shorter wavelengths.
  • This helps explain why blue stars are hotter than red stars.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Wien → Hotter → Shorter Peak Wavelength

41. Kirchhoff's Law of Thermal Radiation
  • A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter at the same wavelength and temperature.
  • An ideal black body is a perfect absorber and an ideal emitter.
  • Gustav Kirchhoff contributed importantly to thermal radiation theory.
42. Coulomb's Law
  • Coulomb's Law describes electrostatic force between point charges.
  • Electrostatic force is directly proportional to the product of the charges.
  • It is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
  • Like charges repel.
  • Unlike charges attract.
  • Charles-Augustin de Coulomb formulated the law.
  • The SI unit of electric charge is coulomb.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Coulomb → Electrostatic Force → Inverse Square

43. Law of Conservation of Electric Charge
  • Total electric charge in an isolated system remains constant.
  • Electric charge can be transferred from one body to another.
  • Charge is not created or destroyed in ordinary processes.
  • Positive and negative charges may be produced in equal amounts through charge separation.
44. Ohm's Law
  • Ohm's Law relates voltage, current and resistance.
  • At constant physical conditions, current through a conductor is proportional to potential difference.
  • V = IR.
  • V is potential difference.
  • I is current.
  • R is resistance.
  • Georg Simon Ohm formulated the law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ohm → V = IR

45. Joule's Law of Heating
  • Electrical current produces heat in a resistor.
  • Heat produced is proportional to the square of current.
  • H = I²Rt.
  • It can also be written as H = VIt.
  • Joule heating is used in electric heaters, irons and toasters.
  • James Prescott Joule is associated with the law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Joule Heating → H = I²Rt

46. Kirchhoff's Current Law
  • Kirchhoff's Current Law is based on conservation of electric charge.
  • At a junction, total current entering equals total current leaving.
  • It is also called the junction rule.
  • Gustav Kirchhoff formulated the circuit laws.
📌 Remember

KCL → Junction → Current

47. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law
  • Kirchhoff's Voltage Law is based on conservation of energy.
  • The algebraic sum of potential differences around a closed circuit loop is zero.
  • It is also called the loop rule.
📌 Remember

KVL → Loop → Voltage

48. Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction
  • Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction.
  • An emf is induced when magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes.
  • Greater rate of change of magnetic flux produces greater induced emf.
  • Electric generators operate on electromagnetic induction.
  • Transformers operate using electromagnetic induction between coils.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Faraday → Changing Magnetic Flux → Induced EMF

49. Lenz's Law
  • Lenz's Law gives the direction of induced current.
  • The induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it.
  • Heinrich Lenz formulated the law.
  • Lenz's Law is consistent with conservation of energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lenz → Induced Current Opposes Change

50. Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis
  • Faraday formulated quantitative laws of electrolysis.
  • The mass of substance deposited at an electrode is proportional to the quantity of electricity passed.
  • For the same quantity of electricity, deposited masses are related to their chemical equivalent masses.
  • Electrolysis converts electrical energy into chemical change.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Faraday's electromagnetic induction → Magnetism and electricity.

Faraday's electrolysis laws → Chemical effects of electric current.

51. Ampère's Circuital Law
  • Ampère's circuital law relates magnetic fields to electric currents.
  • Electric current produces a magnetic field.
  • André-Marie Ampère made major contributions to electromagnetism.
  • The ampere, SI unit of electric current, is named after him.
52. Biot-Savart Law
  • The Biot-Savart law describes the magnetic field produced by a current element.
  • Magnetic field strength depends on current, geometry and distance.
  • Jean-Baptiste Biot and Félix Savart are associated with the law.
53. Laws of Magnetic Poles
  • Like magnetic poles repel.
  • Unlike magnetic poles attract.
  • Isolated magnetic poles have not been observed in ordinary magnets.
  • Cutting a bar magnet produces smaller magnets, each with north and south poles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Magnetic poles → Like repel, unlike attract

54. Laws of Reflection
  • The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
  • The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane.
  • Angles are measured from the normal.
  • Reflection occurs from mirrors and many other surfaces.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Reflection → i = r

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Angle is measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.

55. Snell's Law of Refraction
  • Snell's Law describes refraction of light between two media.
  • n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.
  • Refractive index determines how light bends at a boundary.
  • Willebrord Snell is associated with the law.
  • Light generally bends toward the normal when entering a medium of higher refractive index from a lower one.
  • Light bends away from the normal when moving to a lower refractive index.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Snell → Refraction → n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r

56. Laws of Refraction
  • The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane.
  • For a given pair of media, sin i/sin r is constant for monochromatic light.
  • This constant is related to refractive index.
  • Refraction occurs because the speed of light changes between media.
57. Total Internal Reflection
  • Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser optical medium to a rarer optical medium.
  • The angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.
  • No refracted ray then emerges into the second medium.
  • Optical fibres work using total internal reflection.
  • Sparkling of diamonds is enhanced by total internal reflection.
📌 Must-Memorise Conditions

Denser → Rarer

Angle of incidence > Critical angle

58. Huygens' Principle
  • Every point on a wavefront can be considered a source of secondary wavelets.
  • The new wavefront is the envelope of these secondary wavelets.
  • Christiaan Huygens proposed the wave theory of light.
  • Huygens' principle helps explain reflection and refraction.
59. Principle of Superposition of Waves
  • When two or more waves overlap, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of individual displacements.
  • Superposition produces interference.
  • Constructive interference increases resultant amplitude.
  • Destructive interference reduces resultant amplitude.
60. Doppler Effect
  • The Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between source and observer.
  • Approaching source and observer produce higher observed frequency.
  • Receding motion produces lower observed frequency.
  • The Doppler effect occurs with sound and electromagnetic waves.
  • Radar speed measurement uses Doppler principles.
  • Astronomical redshift and blueshift are related to changes in observed wavelength.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Approaching → Higher frequency

Receding → Lower frequency

61. Principle of Resonance
  • Resonance occurs when a system is driven near its natural frequency.
  • Resonance can produce large-amplitude oscillations.
  • Musical instruments make use of resonance.
  • Radio tuning uses electrical resonance.
  • Excessive resonance can damage structures.
62. Law of Simple Pendulum
  • For small oscillations, the time period of a simple pendulum is T = 2π√(L/g).
  • Time period depends on length and gravitational acceleration.
  • For small oscillations, time period does not depend on mass of the bob.
  • Increasing length increases the time period.
  • Increasing gravitational acceleration decreases the time period.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Pendulum period → Independent of bob mass for ideal small oscillations.

63. Laws of Friction
  • Friction opposes relative motion or tendency of relative motion between surfaces.
  • Static friction acts before sliding begins.
  • Limiting friction is the maximum value of static friction.
  • Kinetic friction acts when surfaces slide.
  • Rolling friction is generally smaller than sliding friction.
  • Friction depends strongly on the nature and condition of surfaces.
64. Conservation of Angular Momentum
  • Angular momentum remains constant when no external torque acts on a system.
  • A spinning skater rotates faster by pulling the arms inward.
  • Planetary motion also demonstrates angular-momentum conservation.
  • Angular momentum is important in rotating systems.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

No External Torque → Angular Momentum Conserved

65. Principle of Moments
  • For a body in rotational equilibrium, clockwise moment equals anticlockwise moment about the pivot.
  • Moment of force = Force × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • The SI unit of moment is newton metre.
  • Levers operate using the principle of moments.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Equilibrium → Clockwise Moment = Anticlockwise Moment

66. Law of Lever
  • A lever is in equilibrium when effort × effort arm equals load × load arm.
  • Mechanical advantage = Load/Effort.
  • Levers may be first-, second- or third-class depending on the positions of fulcrum, load and effort.
67. Conservation of Mechanical Energy
  • In the absence of non-conservative forces such as friction, total mechanical energy remains constant.
  • Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energy.
  • At maximum height, gravitational potential energy may be maximum.
  • During falling, potential energy converts into kinetic energy.
  • Friction converts some mechanical energy into thermal energy.
68. Work-Energy Theorem
  • Net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
  • Wnet = ΔKE.
  • Positive net work increases kinetic energy.
  • Negative net work decreases kinetic energy.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Net Work → Change in Kinetic Energy

69. Principle of Conservation of Linear Momentum in Collisions
  • Total linear momentum is conserved in an isolated collision.
  • Momentum is conserved in both elastic and inelastic collisions.
  • Kinetic energy is conserved in an ideal elastic collision.
  • Kinetic energy is not conserved as kinetic energy in an inelastic collision.
  • In a perfectly inelastic collision, colliding bodies stick together.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Momentum → Conserved in isolated elastic and inelastic collisions.

Kinetic energy → Conserved only in elastic collisions.

70. Lavoisier's Role in Chemistry
  • Antoine Lavoisier is called one of the founders of modern chemistry.
  • He established the quantitative importance of conservation of mass.
  • Lavoisier helped replace the phlogiston theory with oxygen-based explanations of combustion.
  • He recognised oxygen's role in combustion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lavoisier → Modern Chemistry + Conservation of Mass

71. Dalton's Atomic Theory — Key Laws Link
  • John Dalton developed an early modern atomic theory.
  • Dalton's theory explained the laws of chemical combination.
  • Matter was proposed to consist of atoms.
  • Atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.
  • Modern atomic theory has modified some of Dalton's original assumptions.
  • Atoms of the same element can differ in mass because isotopes exist.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Dalton's statement that all atoms of one element have identical mass is not strictly valid because of isotopes.

72. Hess's Law
  • Hess's Law deals with heat changes in chemical reactions.
  • Total enthalpy change depends only on initial and final states.
  • It does not depend on the pathway taken.
  • Hess's Law is an application of conservation of energy.
  • It is useful for calculating enthalpy changes that are difficult to measure directly.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hess → Enthalpy Change Independent of Path

73. Le Chatelier's Principle
  • Le Chatelier's Principle applies to systems at chemical equilibrium.
  • When an equilibrium system is disturbed, it shifts in a direction that tends to oppose the disturbance.
  • Changes in concentration can shift equilibrium.
  • Changes in pressure affect equilibria involving gases when the numbers of gaseous moles differ.
  • Changes in temperature can shift equilibrium.
  • A catalyst speeds attainment of equilibrium but does not change the equilibrium position.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Catalyst → Does not shift equilibrium.

74. Law of Chemical Equilibrium
  • At equilibrium, forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
  • Concentrations remain constant with time at equilibrium, though molecular reactions continue.
  • Chemical equilibrium is dynamic, not static.
  • Equilibrium constant depends on temperature for a given reaction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Equilibrium → Forward Rate = Reverse Rate

75. Raoult's Law
  • Raoult's Law relates vapour pressure to mole fraction in an ideal solution.
  • Partial vapour pressure of a component is proportional to its mole fraction.
  • François-Marie Raoult formulated the law.
  • Addition of a non-volatile solute lowers the vapour pressure of a solvent.
76. Henry's Law
  • Henry's Law relates gas solubility in a liquid to gas pressure above the liquid.
  • At constant temperature, dissolved gas concentration is proportional to its partial pressure for dilute solutions under suitable conditions.
  • William Henry formulated the law.
  • Carbonated beverages use high pressure to dissolve carbon dioxide.
  • Gas solubility generally decreases when pressure is reduced.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Henry → Gas Solubility ∝ Pressure

77. Beer-Lambert Law
  • Beer-Lambert Law relates absorption of light to concentration and path length.
  • Absorbance is proportional to concentration for suitable dilute solutions.
  • Spectrophotometry uses the Beer-Lambert relationship.
  • The law is widely used in chemical analysis.
78. Mendel's Law of Segregation
  • Gregor Mendel is called the Father of Genetics.
  • The Law of Segregation states that the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation.
  • Each gamete receives one allele for a gene.
  • Fertilisation restores the pair of alleles.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mendel → Segregation → Alleles Separate

79. Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment
  • Alleles of different genes assort independently during gamete formation when the genes are sufficiently unlinked.
  • The law does not apply universally to genes located close together on the same chromosome.
  • Genetic linkage can produce deviations from independent assortment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Independent assortment is not absolute for all genes because linked genes exist.

80. Mendel's Principle of Dominance
  • In a simple Mendelian heterozygote, one allele may determine the observed phenotype over another.
  • The expressed allele is called dominant.
  • The masked allele is called recessive.
  • Not all genetic traits show complete dominance.
  • Incomplete dominance and codominance are important exceptions to simple dominance patterns.
81. Hardy-Weinberg Principle
  • The Hardy-Weinberg principle describes allele and genotype frequencies in an ideal non-evolving population.
  • Allele frequencies remain constant when specific assumptions are met.
  • Major assumptions include very large population, random mating, no mutation, no migration and no natural selection.
  • For two alleles, p + q = 1.
  • Genotype frequencies are represented by p² + 2pq + q² = 1.
  • Deviations can indicate evolutionary forces.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hardy-Weinberg → Genetic Equilibrium

82. Gause's Competitive Exclusion Principle
  • Two species competing for exactly the same limiting resources cannot indefinitely occupy exactly the same ecological niche under stable conditions.
  • One may outcompete the other or niche differentiation may occur.
  • Georgy Gause is associated with the principle.
  • Resource partitioning can allow similar species to coexist.
83. Liebig's Law of the Minimum
  • Growth is limited by the essential resource that is in shortest supply relative to need.
  • Justus von Liebig is associated with the law.
  • The law is important in plant nutrition and ecology.
  • Increasing a resource that is not limiting may have little effect until the limiting factor is addressed.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Liebig → Growth Limited by Scarcest Essential Factor

84. Shelford's Law of Tolerance
  • Organisms have minimum and maximum tolerance limits for environmental factors.
  • Survival and abundance depend on remaining within suitable tolerance ranges.
  • Victor Shelford is associated with the law.
  • Temperature, salinity, moisture and pH can act as limiting environmental factors.
85. Biogenetic Law — Historical Note
  • Ernst Haeckel proposed the phrase “ontogeny recapitulates phylogeny.”
  • It suggested that embryonic development repeats evolutionary history.
  • The strict form of this so-called biogenetic law is not accepted in modern biology.
  • Embryology nevertheless provides evidence useful in evolutionary biology.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Haeckel's strict recapitulation law is historically important but not accepted literally in modern biology.

86. Gresham's Law — Cross-Disciplinary Fact
  • Gresham's Law states that “bad money drives out good money” under particular monetary conditions.
  • It is an economic law rather than a natural-science law.
  • It is associated with Sir Thomas Gresham.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Gresham's Law → Economics, not General Science.

87. Moore's Law — Technology Fact
  • Moore's Law is an empirical observation about growth in transistor density in integrated circuits.
  • It is associated with Gordon Moore.
  • It is not a fundamental law of nature.
  • The historical observation suggested transistor counts on integrated circuits would increase rapidly over time.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Moore's Law → Technological trend, not physical law.

  • Conservation of Angular Momentum → No external torque.
  • Conservation of Electric Charge → Isolated system.
  • Mass-energy conservation → Relativistic and nuclear processes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Conservation Laws → Fundamental organizing principles of science

  • Dalton → Total pressure = Sum of partial pressures.
  • Graham → Lighter gas diffuses faster.

97. TNPSC Traps
  • Scientific law and scientific theory are not stages of the same hierarchy.
  • Newton's First Law is the Law of Inertia.
  • Action and reaction act on different bodies.
  • Momentum is conserved in an isolated system.
  • Kinetic energy is not necessarily conserved in an inelastic collision.
  • Mass is conserved in ordinary closed-system chemical reactions.
  • E = mc² describes mass-energy equivalence.
  • Gravitational and electrostatic forces both follow inverse-square relationships.
  • Hooke's Law applies only within the elastic limit.
  • Pascal's Law concerns pressure transmission in confined fluids.
  • Archimedes' Principle concerns buoyant force.
  • Boyle's Law requires constant temperature.
  • Charles's Law requires constant pressure.
  • Gay-Lussac's pressure law requires constant volume.
  • Gas-law temperatures must use an absolute temperature scale.
  • Avogadro's Law concerns amount of gas and volume at constant T and P.
  • Zeroth Law concerns thermal equilibrium.
  • First Law concerns conservation of energy.
  • Second Law concerns direction of spontaneous processes and entropy.
  • Third Law concerns behaviour near absolute zero.
  • Ohm's Law is V = IR under constant physical conditions.
  • KCL concerns current; KVL concerns voltage.
  • Faraday's Law gives induced emf; Lenz's Law gives its direction.
  • Angle of reflection is measured from the normal.
  • Total internal reflection requires travel from optically denser to rarer medium.
  • A catalyst does not alter the equilibrium position.
  • Mendel's Independent Assortment does not apply perfectly to tightly linked genes.
